claims.text: Protective oxide formation and persistence in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C are controlled by the interplay between element-specific oxidation kinetics and oxide/metal lattice mismatch.
CrFeCoNiAl preferentially forms Al2O3 during high-temperature oxidative or corrosive exposure.
CrFeCoNiSi preferentially forms SiO2 during high-temperature oxidative or corrosive exposure.
The Al2O3 and SiO2 scales formed on these alloys have relatively low diffusivity.
The Al2O3 and SiO2 scales formed on these alloys are well matched to the metal substrate and therefore generate relatively low interfacial strain.
Low oxide diffusivity and low oxide/metal interfacial strain promote formation of an adherent, persistent protective scale.
CrFeCoNiMn tends to form mixed oxides with higher diffusion rates and greater oxide/metal lattice mismatch than the Al- or Si-containing variants.
A multiphase metallic microstructure enhances elemental diffusion relative to a single-phase microstructure.
Interfacial heterogeneity in multiphase alloys increases mechanical strain at the oxide/metal interface.
Enhanced diffusion and interfacial strain in multiphase alloys promote oxide cracking or spallation.
Single-phase CrFeCoNiAl and CrFeCoNiSi will form more stable, coherent, and adherent protective scales than single-phase CrFeCoNiMn.
For a given X element, a multiphase CrFeCoNiX alloy will exhibit more oxide cracking or spallation than its single-phase counterpart.
Controlled heat treatments can be used to produce both single-phase and multiphase states in the proposed CrFeCoNiX alloy series.
Single-phase CrFeCoNiMn is the defined comparison baseline.
The proposed hypothesis is restricted to oxidative or corrosive exposure above 900 °C and does not address lower temperatures or non-aggressive environments.
